en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Familiarity within the Section of Puzzling Questions (Meṇḍakapañha)
8. The Question on the Discourse to the Brahmin King “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Tathāgata: ‘Monks, I am a brahmin devoted to begging.
Yet, on the other hand, it was also said:”
“I am a king, O Sela.
If, venerable Nāgasena, it was said by the Blessed One:
“I am a brahmin, O monks, devoted to begging,” then that statement, “I am a king, O Sela,” must be false.
“If it was said by the Tathāgata, ‘I am a king, Sela,’ then the statement, ‘Bhikkhus, I am a brahmin devoted to sacrifice,’ must also be false.
For whether one be a khattiya or a brahmin, there cannot be two castes within a single birth. This too is a double-pronged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.”
“Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, I am a brahmin devoted to begging,’ and yet it was also said:
‘I am a king, O Sela. There is a reason for this, by which the Tathāgata is both a brahmin and a king.”
“But what, venerable Nāgasena, is that reason by which the Tathāgata is both a brahmin and a king?

“Great King, all evil, unwholesome states have been banished, abandoned, removed, dispelled, cut off, exhausted, brought to destruction, extinguished, and stilled in the Tathāgata; therefore the Tathāgata is called a ‘brahmin.’”

One called a *brāhmaṇa* has transcended doubt, multiplicity of views, and the path of uncertainty; the Blessed One too, Great King, has transcended doubt, multiplicity of views, and the path of uncertainty—for that reason the Tathāgata is called a “*brāhmaṇa*.
One called a *brāhmaṇa* has emerged from all states of existence, destinies, and wombs; he is free from stain and dust, and is without companion;
the Blessed One too, Great King, has emerged from all states of existence, destinies, and wombs; he is free from stain and dust, and is without companion—for that reason...
The Tathāgata is called a "brahmin.

One who is called a brahmin is preeminent, most excellent, supreme, and sublime in divine abiding; and the Blessed One, Great King, is likewise preeminent, most excellent, supreme, and sublime in divine abiding. For that reason also, the Tathāgata is called a "brahmin.

One who is called a brahmin is a bearer of the lineage and tradition of former instruction, consisting of study and teaching, giving and receiving, self-restraint, moderation, and observance of rules.

The Blessed One, O Great King, maintains the lineage, tradition, and succession of the former Conquerors— consisting of study, teaching, receiving gifts, giving, self-restraint, moderation, and observance of rules—
and for that reason the Tathāgata is called a "brahmin. A brahmin, indeed,
is one who meditates upon the jhānas of sublime happiness.
The Blessed One, Great King, is a meditator who dwells in the meditative absorption of sublime happiness; for that reason also, the Tathāgata is called a “brahmin.
One who is called a brahmin knows the noble birth, conduct, and behavior throughout all states of existence and non-existence;
the Blessed One, Great King, likewise knows the noble birth, conduct, and behavior throughout all states of existence and non-existence—for that reason also [he is called a brahmin].
The Tathāgata is called a "brahmin.
As for the term "brahmin," Great King, this is not a name given to the Blessed One by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother,
nor by his sister, nor by his friends and ministers, nor by his kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins.
It was not made by humans, nor was it made by deities; this name of the Blessed Buddhas is definitive.
It was established upon the very root of the Bodhi tree after they had shattered the army of Māra and excluded all past, future, and present evil, unwholesome states.
It is a realization-based designation that became manifest and arose simultaneously with the attainment of omniscient knowledge.
“Because he is a brahmin, for that reason the Tathāgata is called ‘brahmin.
“But by what reason, venerable Nāgasena, is the Tathāgata called ‘king’?
“O Great King, one who exercises sovereignty and instructs the world is called a king. And the Blessed One, O Great King, likewise—”
He rules by Dhamma over a world-system of ten thousand worlds;
he governs the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its princes and its people. For that reason also, the Tathāgata is called “King.
As for what is called a king, O Great King: having overcome all people and men, he brings joy to his circle of kinsmen and causes [his enemies] to grieve.
He raises aloft a bright, stainless white parasol— firm, with a strong shaft, and adorned with no fewer than a hundred ribs—
which robs the host of enemies of their great fame and glory; and so too, O Great King, the Blessed One,

grieving the army of Māra who has practiced wrongly and gladdening gods and humans who have practiced rightly, [raises aloft] that which robs the ten-thousandfold world-system of its great fame and glory.
He raises aloft the white, stainless, and pure parasol of supreme liberation, which has patience for its firm and strong handle and is adorned with the hundred excellent spokes of knowledge;
for that reason also, the Tathāgata is called a “king.

Furthermore, one who is called a king is to be honored by the many people who have come to him for prosperity; likewise, Great King, the Blessed One is to be honored by the many gods and humans who have come to him for prosperity—for that reason also, the Tathāgata is called a “king.”
A king, having become pleased with anyone who has gratified him, satisfies that person with whatever boon they have requested by fulfilling their desire;

so too, Great King, the Blessed One, having become pleased with anyone who has gratified him through body, speech, or mind, gives them the unsurpassed boon of liberation from all suffering as their chosen boon, and thus satisfies them with the boon of the complete cessation of all desires. For this reason also...
The Tathāgata is called “the King.
Now, a king indeed rebukes, punishes, and destroys one who transgresses his command;
likewise, Great King, one who transgresses the command in the Blessed One’s excellent teaching becomes shamed by a sense of moral dread, being despised, reviled, and censured, and thus he suffers.
Because he has emerged from the supreme teaching of the Jina, for that reason also the Tathāgata is called “the King.

One who is called a king, by following the lineage and instructions of former righteous kings, illuminating what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma, and exercising sovereignty righteously, becomes beloved, dear, and desired by the people; he maintains the royal lineage for a long time.

By the power of the qualities of the Dhamma, O Great King, the Blessed One likewise—following the lineage and instruction of the former Self-Existent Ones, illuminating what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma, and governing the world according to the Dhamma—is beloved, dear, and longed for by gods and humans;
and by the power of the qualities of the Dhamma, he causes his teaching to endure for a long time. For that reason also, the Tathāgata is called a "king."
"In this way, Great King, there are manifold reasons by which a Tathāgata might be a brahmin and might also be a king;
even a most skillful monk could not establish such a case even in an eon. What is the use of speaking too much?
You should accept it in brief."
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! This is so; thus do I accept it.
Thus ends the eighth dilemma, the Discussion on the Brahmin King.
